newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden's finance minister defends hesitancy on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's finance minister defends hesitancy on EMU.

text.p: Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink on Friday defended his government's open mind on the European economic and monetary union (EMU) as the nation's industries and unions remained divided on membership.

"The choice of exchange rate policies in Sweden depends on parliament's decision in the autumn of 1997 about whether we will take part in the currency union EMU or not," Asbrink said in a parliamentary debate.
"The important things for international confidence are sound and credible economic policies."
Asbrink said if Sweden decided to join EMU then it would have to quickly consider linking the crown to the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

But he said if parliament opposed membership it would then need to decide whether Sweden should join the new exchange rate mechanism, ERM2, planned for European Union (EU) countries that remained outside the EMU.

Sweden's minority Social Democrats government has refrained from expressing a party line on EMU, calling for debate and referring the issue to its party congress in September this year. This will be followed by a parliamentary decision.

But while the government procrastinates, Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, and a large part of the nation's industry are pushing for Sweden to be among the first batch of countries to join EMU at the start on January 1, 1999.
The Riksbank a week ago dismissed an offical government commission into EMU membership, led by Lars Calmfors, that concluded Sweden should not join EMU at the start but wait to see how it develops.

"The economic benefits and the possibility of influencing the future direction of monetary policy leads the Riksbank's governing board to conclude that Sweden should participate in the EMU from the start," the Riksbank said.

Industry this week backed the Riksbank's stance with the associations for Swedish insurers and Swedish wholesalers as well as the country's Export Council expressing support for Sweden joining EMU from the start.

"EMU membership will have a positive effect on the chances for small and mid-sized Swedish companies to grow," said Export Council's head Ulf Dinkenspiel. "At the same time those who already are exporters will be able to increase their exports."
The Finance Inspectorate remained on the fence in its reply to the Calmfors Commission but said EMU membership would be positive for Swedish companies and households.
The general population has started to warm to the idea of EMU membership after earlier fierce opposition.

A January 22 poll showed 23 percent of respondees were in favour of joining EMU at the start compared to 18 percent in a similar poll in November. However 39 percent still remained opposed to EMU membership.
Swedish unions have spoken out against joining the EMU.
Umbrella union body LO and Sweden's Labour Market Board (AMS) said Sweden should wait to join because of the current high unemployment.
"The LO's top priority is full employment," LO said in a statement.
